title: Shamonda Virus (SHAV): Taxonomy, Ecology, Emergence in Europe, Human Infection and Prospects for Pharmacological Intervention – A Narrative Review
content: Background. Shamonda virus (SHAV) is a midge-borne orthobunyavirus of the Simbu serogroup that, until 2026, was known mainly as a sporadic veterinary pathogen in Africa and Asia. In summer 2026 two novel clades, SHAV-EU1 and SHAV-EU2, emerged across Europe, and on 22 October 2026 France reported the first documented human infection. Objective. To review the taxonomy, virology, ecology, epidemiology, veterinary disease, human infection, diagnostics and candidate pharmacological interventions for SHAV. Methods. Narrative review of peer-reviewed articles, preprints and official agency communications (WHO, ECDC, national veterinary authorities) available to 6 November 2026. Findings. SHAV is an enveloped, tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA virus transmitted mainly by Culicoides biting midges. In ruminants it causes a febrile, diarrhoeal illness with milk-yield loss in adults and abortion, stillbirth and congenital malformations after transplacental infection; neurological disease has been described in horses. The first human case was a patient in their sixties, profoundly immunosuppressed after alemtuzumab and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation, who developed fatal encephalitis; SHAV-EU1 RNA was present in blood for at least two months before onset and reached very high loads in the central nervous system. No SHAV-specific antiviral or vaccine exists. Nucleoside analogues (favipiravir, 2′-fluoro-2′-deoxycytidine, ribavirin), fusion-inhibitory peptides and interferon-induced Mx1 show activity against related bunyaviruses, but evidence for SHAV itself is absent and, in neuroinvasive mouse models, antivirals have prolonged survival rather than prevented death. Conclusion. SHAV has moved from a regional veterinary concern to a One Health problem. Priorities are vector and vector-competence studies, specific serology, systematic surveillance of immunocompromised patients and of blood and transplant safety, and early in vitro and animal testing of candidate antivirals.
